course: Small Machines & Pharmaceuticals: The Complete Import Business

lessons.title: SONCAP for Nigeria
lessons.body: SONCAP stands for Standards Organisation of Nigeria Conformity Assessment Programme. It is mandatory for most regulated products entering Nigeria, including small machines and pharmaceuticals. Without a SONCAP certificate, your goods will be stuck at the port and you may pay hefty demurrage fees. The process starts with a Product Certificate (PC), which you obtain before shipping. The PC is issued after testing your product in an accredited lab. It is valid for three years if you keep importing the same product from the same factory. For each shipment, you then apply for a SONCAP Certificate (SC) using the PC. The SC is what customs officials check. To get the PC, you need to submit test reports, invoices, and a Request for Certificate (RFC) to a SONCAP-accredited agency like SGS, Intertek, or Bureau Veritas. They will review your documents and may inspect the goods at the factory. Fees for a PC range from $500 to $1,500 depending on product complexity. The SC costs about 0.5% of the FOB value, with a minimum of $200. Timelines: PC takes 5-10 working days; SC takes 2-3 days after submitting the PC and shipping documents. Be careful: fake SONCAP certificates are common. Always verify the certificate number on SON's website. Also, ensure your product meets Nigerian standards, like NIS 123 for electrical appliances. If your product fails, you must fix it and retest. Budget for these costs and time in your import plan. Many importers fail because they skip the PC and try to get the SC directly, which is impossible. Start early: get your PC before you even order goods. That way, you avoid delays. For pharmaceuticals, you also need NAFDAC registration, which is separate but often runs parallel. In summary, SONCAP is a two-step process: PC then SC. Use accredited agencies, verify certificates, and factor in 2-4 weeks total. This protects your business and ensures smooth clearance.

lessons.title: PVoC for Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda
lessons.body: PVoC stands for Pre-Export Verification of Conformity. It is required for regulated products entering Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda. The goal is to ensure goods meet local standards before they leave the exporting country. For small machines and pharmaceuticals, you must get a Certificate of Conformity (CoC) from an accredited agency like SGS, Intertek, or Bureau Veritas. The process: first, check if your product is regulated. In Kenya, for example, most electrical goods, toys, and chemicals are regulated. You then contact an agency and submit a Request for Certification (RFC) with proforma invoice, test reports, and product details. The agency reviews and may inspect the goods at the factory. If all is well, they issue a CoC. Without a CoC, your goods will be rejected at the port, and you may have to re-export them at your own cost. Costs: for a 20-foot container of small machines, expect $500-$1,200 for inspection and certification. The fee is based on FOB value, typically 0.5% to 1%, with a minimum of $300. Timelines: 5-10 working days for document review, plus inspection scheduling. In Kenya, PVoC is mandatory for all regulated products. Tanzania has a similar program called PVoC, and Uganda uses PVoC as well. Each country has its own list of regulated products, so check the respective standards body: KEBS for Kenya, TBS for Tanzania, and UNBS for Uganda. A common mistake is assuming one CoC works for all three countries. It does not. You need a separate CoC for each destination. Also, some products are exempt, like raw materials for manufacturing, but you must prove that. For pharmaceuticals, you also need registration with the national drug authority, like PPB in Kenya. To save time, work with an agency that has offices in your country and in the destination country. They can guide you on specific requirements. Always verify the agency is accredited by the destination country's standards body. For example, in Kenya, only agencies recognized by KEBS can issue CoCs. Budget 2-3 weeks for the entire process. If you ship without a CoC, you risk confiscation and fines. So, plan ahead. Get your test reports ready early, and ensure your supplier cooperates with the inspection. This will make your import smooth and profitable.

lessons.title: NRCS for South Africa
lessons.body: NRCS stands for National Regulator for Compulsory Specifications. It is the body that enforces compulsory specifications for certain products in South Africa, including electrical appliances, automotive components, and some chemicals. For small machines and pharmaceuticals, you need to check if your product falls under NRCS regulations. If it does, you must obtain a Letter of Authority (LOA) before shipping. The LOA is issued by NRCS after they approve your test reports and factory inspection. The process: first, identify the applicable compulsory specification, like VC 8008 for electrical appliances. Then, submit an application to NRCS with test reports from an accredited lab, product samples if required, and a declaration of conformity. NRCS may conduct a factory inspection or require an inspection by an approved agency. Fees: application fee is around R2,000 to R5,000, and testing can cost R10,000 to R50,000 depending on the product. Timelines: 4-8 weeks for LOA approval. Once you have the LOA, you can import. But each shipment must be accompanied by a Certificate of Conformity (CoC) issued by an accredited agency like SGS or Intertek. The CoC is based on the LOA and verifies that the goods match the approved type. Without a CoC, customs will not clear your goods. For pharmaceuticals, you also need registration with SAHPRA (South African Health Products Regulatory Authority), which is separate and more stringent. A common pitfall is assuming that a CE or ISO certificate is enough. It is not. NRCS requires South African-specific approval. Also, the LOA is product-specific and factory-specific, so if you change supplier, you need a new LOA. To avoid delays, start the NRCS process at least 3 months before you plan to ship. Work with a local agent who understands NRCS requirements. They can help you compile the dossier and liaise with NRCS. Costs can be high, but without LOA, your goods will be stuck at the port. So, budget for it. In summary, NRCS is a pre-shipment requirement for regulated products in South Africa. Get your LOA, then CoC per shipment. Verify all documents, and ensure your supplier is compliant. This will protect your investment and keep your business running.

lessons.title: Product Certificate and Certificate of Conformity
lessons.body: In pre-shipment inspection, two key documents are the Product Certificate (PC) and the Certificate of Conformity (CoC). They are often confused, but they serve different purposes. The PC is a long-term approval for a specific product from a specific factory. It is issued after testing and possibly factory inspection. The PC is valid for 1-3 years, depending on the country. For example, in Nigeria's SONCAP, the PC is valid for 3 years. The CoC, on the other hand, is shipment-specific. It confirms that the goods in a particular shipment conform to the approved PC or to the relevant standards. You need a CoC for each shipment. In Kenya's PVoC, the CoC is issued per shipment. In South Africa, the CoC is also per shipment, based on the LOA. So, the PC is like a driver's license, and the CoC is like a vehicle inspection sticker for each trip. To get a PC, you need to submit test reports from an accredited lab, product specifications, and a factory audit report if required. The cost for a PC ranges from $500 to $2,000. The CoC costs about 0.5% of the FOB value, with a minimum of $200-$300. Timelines: PC takes 1-3 weeks; CoC takes 2-5 days after submitting shipping documents. A common mistake is to think that a PC alone is enough for customs clearance. It is not. You must have a CoC for each shipment. Another mistake is to use a PC from a different factory. The PC is tied to the factory, so if you change manufacturers, you need a new PC. Also, ensure that the test reports are recent, usually within 1-2 years. For pharmaceuticals, the PC may be replaced by a marketing authorization or registration certificate. Always check the specific requirements of the destination country. To streamline, work with an agency that can handle both PC and CoC. They can guide you on the required tests and documentation. Keep copies of all certificates and CoCs. Customs officials may ask for them. In summary, PC is for the product, CoC is for the shipment. Both are essential for smooth import. Budget for both and start early. This will save you time and money.

lessons.title: Working with SGS, Intertek, and Bureau Veritas
lessons.body: SGS, Intertek, and Bureau Veritas are the three major global inspection, verification, testing, and certification companies. They are accredited to issue certificates for most African pre-shipment programs, including SONCAP, PVoC, and NRCS. Working with them is essential for compliance. Here's how to work effectively with them. First, choose the right agency for your destination. All three are usually accepted, but sometimes a country's standards body has a preferred list. For example, in Kenya, KEBS recognizes all three. In Nigeria, SONCAP accepts all three. Check the latest list. Second, contact them early. As soon as you have a proforma invoice, reach out to their local office. They will assign a case manager. Provide all documents: proforma invoice, test reports, product details, and factory information. Be honest about the product. If you hide something, you risk rejection. Third, schedule inspections. They may need to inspect the goods at the factory or at a warehouse. For small machines, they check quantity, packaging, labeling, and sometimes performance. For pharmaceuticals, they check batch numbers, expiry dates, and storage conditions. Inspection fees range from $300 to $800 per man-day, plus travel costs if outside major cities. Fourth, pay fees promptly. They typically require payment before issuing certificates. Fees for a CoC are about 0.5% of FOB value, with minimums. Fifth, follow up. After inspection, they issue a draft certificate. Review it carefully for errors. Once approved, they issue the final certificate. Timelines: 3-7 working days for inspection and certificate issuance, but can be longer if there are issues. A common mistake is to wait until goods are at the port to start the process. That leads to demurrage. Start at least 2 weeks before shipment. Also, build a relationship with your case manager. They can advise you on how to avoid common pitfalls. For example, they might tell you that your test reports are outdated or that your labeling needs to include specific warnings. Use their expertise. Finally, keep all records. You may need them for future shipments or audits. In summary, these agencies are your partners in compliance. Work with them early, provide accurate information, and pay on time. This will ensure your goods clear customs without hassle.

lessons.title: Costs and Timelines for Certification
lessons.body: Budgeting for pre-shipment inspection and certification is crucial for your import business. Costs vary by country, product, and agency. Here is a breakdown of typical costs and timelines for small machines and pharmaceuticals. For SONCAP in Nigeria: Product Certificate (PC) costs $500-$1,500, valid 3 years. SONCAP Certificate (SC) costs 0.5% of FOB, min $200. Timeline: PC 5-10 days, SC 2-3 days. Total for first shipment: $700-$1,700 and 1-2 weeks. For PVoC in Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda: Certificate of Conformity (CoC) costs 0.5%-1% of FOB, min $300. Inspection fee $300-$800. Total: $600-$1,200 and 5-10 days. For NRCS in South Africa: Letter of Authority (LOA) costs R2,000-R5,000 plus testing R10,000-R50,000. CoC per shipment costs 0.5% of FOB, min R2,000. Timeline: LOA 4-8 weeks, CoC 3-5 days. Total: R15,000-R60,000 and 1-2 months. For pharmaceuticals, add drug registration costs: NAFDAC in Nigeria $1,000-$5,000, PPB in Kenya $500-$2,000, SAHPRA in South Africa $2,000-$10,000. Timelines: 3-12 months. To reduce costs, consolidate shipments. If you import regularly, get a PC or LOA that covers multiple shipments. Negotiate with agencies for volume discounts. Also, ensure your test reports are from accredited labs; otherwise, you pay for retesting. Timelines can be shortened by preparing documents in advance and using agencies with local presence. A common mistake is to underestimate these costs and timelines. For example, if you don't get a CoC before shipment, you may pay $1,000 in demurrage. So, include certification in your landed cost calculation. For a $10,000 shipment, certification can add 5-15% to your cost. But it's unavoidable. Plan for it. Start the process as soon as you confirm your supplier. Use a checklist: test reports, proforma invoice, application forms, payment. Follow up weekly. Keep buffer time: add 50% to estimated timelines. This will prevent delays. In summary, certification costs money and time, but it's an investment in smooth clearance. Budget $500-$5,000 per shipment depending on country and product. Timelines range from 1 week to 3 months. Be prepared, and you'll succeed.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Pre-Shipment Inspection & Certification for African Importers

Pre-shipment inspection (PSI) and conformity certification are the single most common cause of cargo delays and demurrage costs for African importers of small machines and pharmaceuticals. A shipment of generators, water pumps, or generic medicines that arrives at Lagos, Mombasa, or Durban without the correct certificate will be held, re-exported, or destroyed â and the importer pays for all of it. This lesson is a working reference: what each scheme requires, what it costs, how long it takes, and how to avoid the mistakes that cost real money.

The core logic is the same across the continent. Governments delegate conformity assessment to accredited third-party inspection companies. The exporter arranges inspection before shipment, receives a Certificate of Conformity (CoC), and the CoC is what allows customs to clear the goods. No CoC, no clearance. The schemes differ in name, scope, and process, but the operating principle is identical.

Scheme-by-Scheme Reference

SONCAP (Nigeria). The Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON) runs a three-stage process. First, the manufacturer obtains a Product Certificate (PC) â either PC1 (single shipment, unregistered) or PC2 (registered, valid for one year, cheaper per shipment). Second, for each consignment the exporter applies for a SONCAP Certificate (SC). Third, the SC is presented to Nigeria Customs. Regulated products include electrical goods, generators, tyres, and many pharmaceuticals and medical devices. Without an SC, goods are stuck at Apapa or Tin Can Island and attract storage charges that can exceed the value of the cargo within weeks.

PVoC (Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda). The Pre-Export Verification of Conformity programme requires inspection in the country of supply. The Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS), the Tanzania Bureau of Standards (TBS), and the Uganda National Bureau of Standards (UNBS) all operate PVoC through appointed agents. A CoC must be issued before shipment; goods arriving without one are subject to destination inspection at 15% of CIF value, or rejection. Kenya also runs a separate PVoC for used motor vehicles and a mandatory KEBS Import Standardisation Mark for certain goods.

NRCS (South Africa). The National Regulator for Compulsory Specifications issues a Letter of Authority (LOA) for products covered by compulsory specifications â electrical equipment, some chemicals, and certain health products. Unlike SONCAP and PVoC, the NRCS LOA is typically applied for by the importer, not the exporter, and is issued before the goods ship. South Africa also applies SABS certification for voluntary standards, but the LOA is the legal gate.

Product Certificate vs Certificate of Conformity. A Product Certificate (PC) is a document about a product â it evidences that the model or formulation has been tested and meets the standard. It is reusable across shipments. A Certificate of Conformity (CoC) is a document about a shipment â it confirms that the specific consignment matches the certified product and passes inspection. Confusing the two is the most common error: exporters arrive at the port with a PC and no CoC, and the cargo is refused.

Cost and Timeline Benchmarks

Table 1: Typical certification costs and timelines (indicative, USD)
Scheme / Document Typical Cost Typical Timeline Validity Who Applies
SONCAP Product Certificate (PC2, registered) $1,500 â $4,000 4 â 8 weeks 1 year Exporter / Manufacturer
SONCAP Certificate (SC) per shipment $300 â $900 3 â 7 working days Single shipment Exporter
PVoC Certificate of Conformity (KEBS/TBS/UNBS) $250 â $800 + inspection fee 5 â 10 working days Single shipment Exporter
NRCS Letter of Authority (LOA) R1,500 â R15,000 (~$80 â $800) 3 â 6 weeks 1 â 3 years Importer (SA entity)
Destination inspection (if no CoC) 15% of CIF value + penalties 2 â 6 weeks delay N/A Importer bears cost

Sources: SONCAP fee schedule (Standards Organisation of Nigeria), KEBS PVoC guidelines, TBS and UNBS PVoC procedures, and NRCS tariff of fees. Figures are indicative and vary by product category, consignment value, and inspection agent.

Table 2: Inspection agents and their African mandates
Inspection Company Active In Typical Scope Notes for Importers
SGS Nigeria, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Ghana PVoC, SONCAP, general inspection Largest network; often the default agent for KEBS and SON
Intertek Nigeria, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda PVoC, SONCAP, testing Strong laboratory capacity for electrical and pharma products
Bureau Veritas Nigeria, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, South Africa PVoC, SONCAP, NRCS support Often used for high-value machinery and industrial goods
Cotecna / TÃV / Others Selected markets PVoC for specific countries Check current appointment before contracting â mandates rotate

Sources: official PVoC and SONCAP programme pages of KEBS, TBS, UNBS, and SON, which list appointed inspection agents. Agent mandates are periodically re-tendered; always confirm the current appointment on the regulator's website before paying any inspection fee.

â ï¸ SAFETY AND COMPLIANCE WARNING

Never ship regulated goods â electrical equipment, generators, pharmaceuticals, medical devices, or chemicals â to Nigeria, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, or South Africa without a valid Certificate of Conformity or Letter of Authority issued before shipment. Goods arriving without the correct certificate are routinely seized, re-exported at the importer's expense, or destroyed. There is no retroactive certification for most schemes. Counterfeit or falsified CoCs are a criminal offence and will result in blacklisting of the exporter and importer. Verify every certificate directly with the issuing regulator, not with the agent who sold it to you.

Working with SGS, Intertek, and Bureau Veritas

These three companies handle the majority of African conformity assessment. Practical rules for dealing with them:

  • Get the RFC in early. The Request for Certification should be filed the moment the proforma invoice is signed â not when the container is at the port. Inspection slots fill up, especially in Q4.
  • Match the product description exactly. The description on the invoice, packing list, and RFC must be identical. Discrepancies trigger a documentary review loop that adds one to two weeks.
  • Keep test reports current. For electrical goods and pharmaceuticals, an ISO/IEC 17025-accredited laboratory report is usually required. Reports older than 12â24 months may be rejected.
  • Budget for the inspection fee separately. The CoC fee and the physical inspection fee are often quoted separately. Ask for a full landed certification cost before committing.
  • Use the agent's local office. For NRCS and SONCAP, the local office in Lagos, Nairobi, or Johannesburg can pre-check documents before the file goes to the regional hub.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Confirm the destination scheme: SONCAP (Nigeria), PVoC (Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda), or NRCS LOA (South Africa).
  2. Identify the correct HS code and check whether the product is regulated under the scheme.
  3. Obtain the Product Certificate (PC2 where possible) before the first shipment â it reduces per-shipment cost and time.
  4. File the Request for Certification with the appointed agent at least 10 working days before loading.
  5. Ensure invoice, packing list, and test reports match the product description exactly.
  6. Confirm the Certificate of Conformity is issued before the vessel departs â not after arrival.
  7. Verify the CoC directly with the issuing regulator (SON, KEBS, TBS, UNBS, NRCS) using the certificate number.
  8. Keep digital and physical copies with the shipping documents for customs presentation.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • Standards Organisation of Nigeria â SONCAP Programme
  • Kenya Bureau of Standards â Pre-Export Verification of Conformity (PVoC)
  • Tanzania Bureau of Standards â PVoC and import certification
  • Uganda National Bureau of Standards â PVoC procedures
  • National Regulator for Compulsory Specifications (South Africa) â Letters of Authority

This module is part of Small Machines & Pharmaceuticals: The Complete Import Business by Rise Africa Skills. Figures are indicative and current at the time of writing; always confirm fees, timelines, and agent appointments with the relevant regulator before committing capital.

quiz.q: What does SONCAP stand for?
options: A) Standards Organisation of Nigeria Conformity Assessment Programme
B) South Nigerian Certification and Assessment Program
C) Standards Organisation of Nigeria Certification and Approval Process
D) Nigerian Agency for Conformity Assessment
quiz.explanation: SONCAP is the Standards Organisation of Nigeria Conformity Assessment Programme.

quiz.q: Which document is required for each shipment under SONCAP?
quiz.explanation: The SONCAP Certificate (SC) is issued per shipment, while the PC is for the product.

quiz.q: What is the validity period of a SONCAP Product Certificate?
quiz.explanation: A SONCAP Product Certificate is valid for three years if the product and factory remain the same.

quiz.q: Which agency is NOT typically accredited for SONCAP?
quiz.explanation: Local customs offices do not issue SONCAP certificates; only accredited agencies like SGS, Intertek, and Bureau Veritas do.

quiz.q: What is the minimum cost for a SONCAP Certificate?
quiz.explanation: The SONCAP Certificate costs about 0.5% of FOB value with a minimum of $200.

quiz.q: What does PVoC stand for?
quiz.explanation: PVoC is Pre-Export Verification of Conformity, required for Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda.

quiz.q: Which country does NOT use PVoC?
quiz.explanation: Nigeria uses SONCAP, not PVoC.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost for a PVoC Certificate of Conformity?
quiz.explanation: PVoC CoC costs about 0.5% to 1% of FOB value, with a minimum of $300.

quiz.q: Which standards body oversees PVoC in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: KEBS is the Kenya Bureau of Standards, which oversees PVoC in Kenya.

quiz.q: How long does a PVoC CoC typically take to issue?
quiz.explanation: PVoC CoC issuance takes about 5-10 working days after document review and inspection.

quiz.q: What does NRCS stand for?
options: A) National Regulator for Compulsory Specifications
B) National Regulatory Commission for Standards
C) Nigerian Regulatory Council for Standards
D) National Registration and Certification Service
quiz.explanation: NRCS is the National Regulator for Compulsory Specifications in South Africa.

quiz.q: What document does NRCS issue for regulated products?
quiz.explanation: NRCS issues a Letter of Authority (LOA) for regulated products before shipment.

quiz.q: What is the approximate timeline for NRCS LOA approval?
quiz.explanation: NRCS LOA approval typically takes 4-8 weeks.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT required for NRCS LOA?
options: A) Test reports from accredited lab
quiz.explanation: A Certificate of Origin is not typically required for NRCS LOA; test reports, factory inspection, and declaration of conformity are.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a Product Certificate (PC) and a Certificate of Conformity (CoC)?
options: A) PC is per shipment, CoC is for the product
B) PC is for the product, CoC is per shipment
D) Both are for the product
quiz.explanation: The PC is a long-term approval for the product, while the CoC is issued for each shipment.

quiz.q: How long is a Product Certificate typically valid?
quiz.explanation: A Product Certificate is usually valid for 1-3 years, depending on the country.

quiz.q: What is the cost of a Certificate of Conformity generally based on?
quiz.explanation: CoC fees are typically a percentage of the FOB value, with a minimum fee.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three major inspection agencies?
quiz.explanation: DHL is a logistics company, not an inspection agency. The big three are SGS, Intertek, and Bureau Veritas.

quiz.q: What should you do first when working with an inspection agency?
options: B) Contact them with proforma invoice and product details
C) Wait for customs to request documents
D) Pay the full fee upfront
quiz.explanation: You should contact the agency early with your proforma invoice and product details to start the certification process.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when dealing with inspection agencies?
options: C) Waiting until goods are at the port to start
quiz.explanation: Waiting until goods are at the port often leads to demurrage and delays; start the process early.

quiz.q: What is the typical inspection fee for SGS, Intertek, or Bureau Veritas?
quiz.explanation: Inspection fees range from $300 to $800 per man-day, plus travel costs if applicable.

quiz.q: Which document must accompany each shipment even after obtaining a Product Certificate?
quiz.explanation: A Certificate of Conformity is required for each shipment, based on the Product Certificate.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost for a SONCAP Product Certificate?
quiz.explanation: SONCAP PC costs between $500 and $1,500 depending on product complexity.

quiz.q: How long does it take to get a SONCAP Certificate after submitting documents?
quiz.explanation: The SONCAP Certificate is typically issued within 2-3 days after submitting the PC and shipping documents.

quiz.q: What additional registration is needed for pharmaceuticals in Nigeria?
quiz.explanation: Pharmaceuticals in Nigeria require NAFDAC registration in addition to SONCAP.

quiz.q: Which of these is a way to reduce certification costs?
quiz.explanation: Consolidating shipments can reduce per-shipment certification costs.

quiz.q: What is the typical timeline for NRCS CoC issuance per shipment?
quiz.explanation: NRCS CoC is typically issued within 3-5 days after submitting required documents.

quiz.q: What should you do if you change your supplier after obtaining a Product Certificate?
options: B) Apply for a new PC
quiz.explanation: The PC is factory-specific, so you need a new PC if you change suppliers.

quiz.q: What is the minimum fee for a PVoC CoC?
quiz.explanation: The PVoC CoC has a minimum fee of $300.

quiz.q: Which of these is a key step in the PVoC process?
options: B) Obtain a Letter of Authority
quiz.explanation: The PVoC process starts with submitting a Request for Certification (RFC) to an accredited agency.
